## Before you begin

Work individually, with nearby discussion if useful. Predict before running each
comparison. All code is supplied; you do not need to write R or Stan code.

Use the prepared browser R environment. If access fails, open this HTML and
[the result sheet](results.html) locally and answer the same questions.
There is one core exercise today. Demonstrations and optional extensions are labelled.
No installation or homework is required in the prepared browser environment.
For optional local use, read [Required packages and setup](../classroom/PACKAGES.md)
before class. No new model fitting is required for the core exercise.

By the end, you should be able to compare predicted survival probabilities and
their uncertainty, and explain why a model should be checked against observations.
The core exercise takes **15 minutes**: predict 2, read/compare 6, write an
interpretation 2, discuss 5. You may run the complete code or use the figures and
[result sheet](results.html); both routes answer the same questions. R and GLM
experience are not prerequisites. The instructor explains the model and checks.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)

source(here("R/functions.R"))
```

# Core exercise: survival at low and high conspecific density

| | |
|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Compare survival probabilities and uncertainty, and explain the ecological result. |
| **Computation** | Supplied posterior draws. Run the completed code or read the supplied figures; no new inference. |
| **Data** | Seedlings and survivors in 60 simulated quadrats, with scaled conspecific density. |

CNDD means conspecific negative density dependence. Today we ask whether seedling
survival probability decreases with conspecific density. These simulated data illustrate
the analysis. They are not observations from the research papers.

## 1. Predict the relationship

```{r core-data}
ndd <- make_ndd_data()
ggplot(ndd, aes(cons, suv/n, size=n)) + geom_point(alpha=.65) +
  labs(x="Conspecific density (scaled)", y="Observed proportion surviving",
       size="Seedlings")
```

Which density would you expect to have higher survival probability? Write a prediction.
Each point is a quadrat. Different quadrats can contain different numbers of seedlings.

## 2. Read the model and curve

The model is the Day 1 binomial model with a density predictor:

$$
s_i \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n_i,p_i), \qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p_i)=\alpha+\beta x_i.
$$

The index $i$ denotes a quadrat. $x_i$ is scaled conspecific density. Both
coefficients have independent Normal priors with mean 0 and **SD** 2.5.
The model assumes a common probability within each quadrat and conditionally
independent survival given that probability.

The instructor will explain this model. You do not need to memorise the logit
formula or learn model-fitting syntax. Load the supplied result below, or use the
curve already displayed in this reading copy.

```{r core-fit}
fit <- course_fit("day2_ndd")
draws <- fit$draws
fit$source
```

`precomputed` means that these draws were generated before class. Loading them
is not running a new fit. They match the data, model and priors described above.

### Compare the two densities

```{r core-curve}
plot_cndd(draws, ndd)
```

Compare low density ($x=-1$, one SD below the mean) with high density ($x=1$, one SD
above the mean). Keep the fitted data, model, prior and draws fixed. Only the
prediction density changes.

```{r core-probabilities}
probabilities <- cndd_probabilities(draws)
probability_summary <- probabilities |> group_by(density) |>
  summarise(median=median(p), lower=quantile(p,.025), upper=quantile(p,.975))
probability_summary
plot_cndd_comparison(draws)
```

## 3. Explain the ecological result

Complete this sentence with values and intervals from the table:

> Predicted survival probability is ___ (95% interval ___ to ___) at low density,
> compared with ___ (___ to ___) at high density, under this model.

Does knowing a survival probability also determine the exact number of survivors
in the next group of seedlings? Explain in one sentence.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

```{r solution-probabilities, echo=FALSE}
lo <- plogis(draws$alpha-draws$beta)
hi <- plogis(draws$alpha+draws$beta)
```

Predicted survival is `r round(median(lo),2)` (`r round(quantile(lo,.025),2)` to
`r round(quantile(lo,.975),2)`) at low density, and `r round(median(hi),2)`
(`r round(quantile(hi,.025),2)` to `r round(quantile(hi,.975),2)`) at high density.
These intervals describe uncertainty about each probability. Future survivor counts
also vary randomly given the probability and the number of seedlings.

The negative density coefficient is on the logit scale. It is neither a probability
difference nor a percent reduction. Transform every draw before summarising the
probability. Hold the predictor values fixed when comparing answers.

This fitted association alone does not establish causation or show why rare species
are rare. Species differences enter the conceptual research example on Day 3.

:::
:::

# Instructor demonstrations: prediction and model checking

The core exercise is complete. Read the following figures with the instructor;
you do not need to run more code.

## Predict new seedling groups

Keep the same fit and compare new groups of **20 seedlings** at the two densities.
The code draws a probability from the posterior and then generates a binomial count.

```{r demo-prediction}
predictions <- cndd_predictions(draws, n=20, seed=20261022)
plot_cndd_predictions(predictions)
```

The probability interval and the distribution of future survivor counts answer
different questions. Counts can vary even if we know the probability precisely.

## Check the model against observations

Keep each observed quadrat's density and seedling count fixed. Generate new
survivor counts using posterior draws. Compare the density pattern and the
range of replicated survival proportions with the observations.

```{r demo-check}
replicates <- cndd_replicates(draws, ndd, seed=20261023)
plot_cndd_check(replicates, ndd)
```

Write one compatible feature and one pattern that would concern you. What would
a systematic mismatch suggest? This is simulation from the existing posterior,
not another model fit.
Because these data were generated from this model, we do not require a visible
failure. A compatible plot alone does not establish ecological adequacy.
Light, soils, shared enemies and species differences may matter in a real study.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

The orange intervals in the first check are intervals for replicated proportions,
including binomial variation at each observed $n_i$. They differ from the interval
for $p_i$ in the fitted-curve plot. Some observed points can lie outside 95% intervals.
Do not count all such points as model failures. Look for systematic patterns.

A discrepancy could involve the density relationship, missing conditions or
dependence among seedlings. It is not a uniquely identified diagnosis of a single
ecological mechanism. The SD summary is optional reference material below.

:::
:::

# Optional reference and lecture illustration

The core exercise is complete. These sections support the lecture; skip them if time is short.

## Prior scale: the Normal regression illustration

The lecture uses the Normal-response example from `main.qmd` to ask whether a
slope of 100 is sensible for the displayed units and ranges. It is a short
illustration, not a second analysis exercise.

```{r demo-normal-prior-scale}
plot_normal_prior_scale()
```

For $y_i\sim\mathcal{N}(a x_i+b,\sigma)$, a slope prior $a\sim\mathcal{N}(0,2.5)$
uses SD 2.5 in the units of $y$ per unit $x$. In CNDD the coefficients are on the
logit scale. The same numerical SD does not imply the same ecological change.
In both models, judge the implied predictions in the units of the question.

## Computation checks: instructor reference

```{r demo-diagnostics}
course_diagnostics(fit)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(draws, pars=c("alpha","beta"))
```

The instructor checks traces, R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, divergences, treedepth and
E-BFMI together. Students only need to distinguish two questions: did computation
work, and does the model describe the observations? Memorising thresholds or
repairing a sampler is not required. Healthy diagnostics do not establish ecological
adequacy. The handwritten Stan model below is reference material, not a coding task.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

# Optional demonstration: fit the same model with brms

**Purpose:** connect the ecological model to one complete fitting command.
**Who/time:** instructor demonstration, up to 3 minutes only if the core discussion
is complete. Use a result prepared before class; omit rather than wait for compilation.
Students with a validated environment may try this later by choice. It is not homework
or a prerequisite for any task. No student installation is required.

`brms` translates an R formula into Stan; `cmdstanr` runs CmdStan.
`0 + Intercept + cons` gives an intercept at cons = 0 and a slope, both with
independent Normal(0, 2.5) priors. This matches `stan/logit_reg.stan`; the usual
centred-intercept specification need not impose the same intercept prior.
The saved core fit is handwritten Stan, not a brms object.

**Starter and instructions:** run setup and core-data above, then this complete
chunk only in a prepared environment. Keep the data, formula and priors fixed.
Compilation and sampling are new computation; elapsed time is machine-dependent
and has not been measured for the classroom server. This chunk is not executed
when rendering the handout. Do not use Run All to start an optional fit.

```{r optional-brms, eval=FALSE}
library(brms)
elapsed <- system.time({
  fit_brms <- brm(
    suv | trials(n) ~ 0 + Intercept + cons,
    data=ndd, family=binomial(link="logit"),
    prior=set_prior("normal(0, 2.5)", class="b"),
    backend="cmdstanr", seed=20261022,
    chains=4, cores=1, iter=2000, warmup=1000, refresh=500
  )
})
elapsed
# Preserve chain/iteration identifiers when adapting names for course plots.
brms_draws <- posterior::subset_draws(
  posterior::as_draws_df(fit_brms), variable=c("b_Intercept", "b_cons"))
names(brms_draws)[names(brms_draws) == "b_Intercept"] <- "alpha"
names(brms_draws)[names(brms_draws) == "b_cons"] <- "beta"
brms_result <- list(draws=brms_draws, data=ndd_stan_data(ndd), source="live-brms",
            diagnostics=fit_brms$fit$diagnostic_summary())
course_diagnostics(brms_result)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(brms_draws, pars=c("alpha", "beta"))
plot_cndd_comparison(brms_draws)
```

**Compare:** expect the same broad density relationship and similar probability
intervals as the supplied fit, with Monte Carlo variation. Report the source as
`live-brms`; loading the saved result is `precomputed`. Check actual live diagnostics
before interpreting a new fit. An error or a problematic fit does not invalidate
your completed core exercise; stop and return to the supplied figures.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

The likelihood, seed data and independent coefficient priors match the core model;
individual draws need not match. `b_Intercept` maps to `alpha`, `b_cons` to `beta`.
Keep chain identifiers for diagnostics. Inspect parameter-level R-hat and ESS,
traces and chain-level sampler diagnostics. Never report healthy stored diagnostics
as diagnostics for a problematic live run. Validate compilation, sampling and
plotting in a fresh instructor account before showing this optional demonstration.

:::
:::

## Optional reference: variation across quadrats

```{r optional-spread}
plot_cndd_spread_check(replicates, ndd)
```

This compares one SD of observed survival proportions with SDs of replicated data.
It is not a posterior distribution for the observed SD. Skip if time is short.

# Optional extension: a probability difference

Use the same fit and paired posterior draws. Compute high-density minus low-density
survival probability, then interpret the distribution. No refit is needed.

```{r optional-difference}
p_low <- plogis(draws$alpha-draws$beta)
p_high <- plogis(draws$alpha+draws$beta)
course_interval(p_high-p_low)
mean(p_high-p_low < 0)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

A negative difference means lower predicted survival at high density for the specified
comparison. The interval comes from paired differences, not from subtracting interval
endpoints. Its units are probability points, not an odds ratio.

:::
:::
